The Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad.
"May He protect us both"—this is the peace mantra (śānti).
The means [of realization] such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth.
Having studied the scriptures and having practiced them again and again, the wise man,
having realized the Supreme Brahman, should cast them aside like a firebrand.
Commentary:
Om. Salutations to the venerable Rāmacandra, the supreme Guru and Great Swan (paramahaṃsa) who is the foundational substratum of the entire universe.
[This is] the Supreme Imperishable (parākṣara), which is the subject matter expounded in the Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad.
May the empire of the bliss of the three steps shine perpetually within my heart.

Indeed, this *Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad* is a branch of the *Kṛṣṇayajurveda*. Its introductory sections and so forth are similar to those of the *Kaṭhavallī* and other texts. A commentary on this Upaniṣad, which consists of the illumination of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), is now begun from a brief text. First, it is stated that for those of pure mind, the attainment of the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) occurs through means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) alone; whereas for those of impure mind, it occurs through knowledge mediated by the practice of the six-limbed yoga, distinguished by the meditation (*upāsanā*) upon Brahman.

(12) The accomplishment of the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha-siddhi*) is expounded in this Upaniṣad. At the outset, it states the means for hearing and so forth for those who are the primary qualified seekers: "The scriptures" (*śāstrāṇi*). Regarding those seeking liberation, the scriptures—known as the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the *Īśa*—provide the instruction that Brahman, established through the negation of everything else, is one's own non-dual Self alone. Having properly studied these from the mouth of a preceptor who is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman, a person of intelligence capable of retaining the meaning of what has been heard should practice them repeatedly until the five defects, such as doubt, are eliminated. By performing hearing, reflection, and meditation without interruption, and through the perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) arising therefrom, one realizes that Brahman—which is the ultimate ground where the entire complex of ignorance and its effects, distinct from oneself, reaches their end and undergoes negation—is one's own non-dual Self alone, because it is the supreme expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of that [Self]. Simultaneous with that knowledge, the wise one attains that state and remains as that alone. Since the study of the scriptures possesses such power, the study of the scriptures must be performed without negligence even after attaining the state of Brahman; therefore, it says: "Like a torch" (*ulkāvat*). Just as one observes an object by the light of a torch and then discards the torch, so too, immediately after attaining the state of Brahman, one should cast aside those scriptures which were the means thereto, as well as the knowledge produced by them. In this regard—
Just as someone holding a torch might discard it after seeing the object [he sought], so too,
having perceived the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should subsequently relinquish that knowledge.
Thus,
having directly realized the Self by means of the self as the perfectly immovable Brahman,
[one abandons] the connections with the body, caste, and so forth, including those associated with the social classes (varṇa) and stages of life (āśrama).
One should cast aside the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Puranas like the dust from one's feet.
And thus says the Śruti. || 1 ||
The meditation on the Praṇava: Having mounted the chariot of the syllable Om and made Viṣṇu the charioteer,
one who is intent on the worship of Rudra seeks the station of the world of Brahmā.
One should travel by chariot only as far as the path for chariots remains;
having reached the end of the chariot path, one leaves the chariot and proceeds on foot.
Having abandoned the measures, genders, and words, and being devoid of vowels and consonants,
one indeed proceeds to the subtle state by means of the vowelless letter *m*.

Having declared the fulfillment of those of the highest qualification by means of the first mantra, [the author] now describes the meditation on the meaning of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) for the sake of those of middling and duller qualifications so that they may ascend to that state—beginning with the words "Oṃkāra... Mounting the *oṃkāra*, which stands in the place of a chariot, one should, preceded by the utterance of the *praṇava*, contemplate its meaning like the resonance of a bronze bell. Having made the intellect-principle (*buddhitattva*), Viṣṇu, the pervasive one, the charioteer—having shaped it into the form of the Lord who is the meaning of the *praṇava*—[one proceeds]. For the scripture says, "Know the intellect to be the charioteer. The "Brahma-world" (*brahmaloka*) is the world of Brahman; it is the Nirviśeṣa Paramātman. Because one attains (*padyate*) that nature, it is called the "Brahma-world-place. Desiring to seek that as one's own true nature, one becomes intent upon the worship of Rudra as the means thereto. He is called "Rudra" because he dissolves (*drāvayati*) the suffering consisting of the plane of one's own ignorance and its effects, which have attained an outward state as something separate from oneself. That "worship of Rudra" (*rudrārādhana*) is the contemplation of "I am the Inner Self" (*pratyagasmīti*), which illumines the existence and non-existence of the thousands of modifications of the individual and collective internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*); it is the state of being solely devoted to that, the meaning of which is "intentness upon that. First, there is the contemplation of the Lord who is the meaning of the *oṃkāra*. When the internal organ is shaped into His form and becomes serene, it seeks to abide as the Nirviśeṣa Brahman alone. As a means to that, there is the contemplation of the Inner Self (*pratyag*). Then, having abandoned the state of the Inner Self which is dependent on the distinction between the inner and the outer, one remains as the non-dual Brahman alone, free from all counter-correlates. This is the intended meaning. || 2 || Since the contemplation of the *praṇava* must be maintained even during the attainment of the state of Brahman, he says "tāvad... (so long as...). As long as one remains on the path of the chariot—the path of contemplating the *praṇava*—one must travel by the chariot; that is, the contemplation of the meaning preceded by the utterance of the *oṃkāra* must be performed. Thus, having stayed at the destination reached by the path of the chariot—that is, having remained as that alone in the Nirviśeṣa Brahman which is the goal to be reached by the path—one then leaves behind the chariot of the *oṃkāra*. Having reached the station of the Turyaturya, one becomes the Turyaturya. This is the meaning. || 3 || He states the means for attaining the Turyaturya: "Mātra... etc. The vowels such as 'A' and others are the causes of all worldly transactions and are the sounds; the consonants beginning with 'Ka' are the syllables. Free from these—meaning devoid of the conceptualization of the phenomenal world consisting of the fifty letters of sound and syllable—is that "word of the Mātrā and Liṅga" (*mātrāliṅgapada*). Having abandoned the forms of the Mātrās (such as 'A'), their presiding deities (Viśva, Virāṭ, Otr), and so forth, and having ascertained that nothing exists apart from oneself, one then, by means of the "soundless" (*asvara*) 'Ma', through the state of the Lord who is the meaning of 'Ma', and by the perfection of the powers of unobstructed action, knowledge, and will, that which is subtle... || 4 ||

That state shines forth; the sage goes to that subtle state which is Brahman as its own self alone (*svamātra*). The meaning is that he remains as Brahman alone, established through the negation (*apahnava*) of all mental constructs consisting of measures (*mātrā*), signs (*liṅga*), words (*śabda*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*). || 4 ||
The definition of withdrawal (pratyāhāra):
One should contemplate the five objects, beginning with sound, as well as the exceedingly fickle mind, as being the rays of one's own self; that is called withdrawal.

He teaches the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) as a cause for the purification of the mind of one whose capacity is dull. Among those, he states the nature of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*): "Sound, etc. In accordance with such scriptural passages as, "Whatever one hears with the two ears, one should contemplate that as the Self," one should contemplate the five objects—sound and so forth—which are perceivable by the ear and other senses, as being rays of one's own Self, which are essentially identical to the Self because they are imagined by the Self. By the word "and" (*ca*) in "and the mind," the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) together with its objects is included. That [mind], however, is extremely fickle because it undergoes change moment by moment. One should contemplate even that as the form of the Self and withdraw it from objects external to the Self; this meaning thus expressed is called withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). (5)
The six-limbed yoga consists of withdrawal of the senses, as well as meditation, breath control, concentration, deliberation, and absorption; this is called the six-limbed yoga. (6)
He enumerates the six limbs of yoga: "Pratyāhāra," etc. The meaning is clear. || 6 ||
Just as the impurities of mountain ores are burned away when they are smelted,
so too the defects produced by the senses are burned away through the practice of breath control (prāṇadhāraṇa). || 7 ||

One should burn away defects through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and sins through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇā). Having brought sin to destruction, one should contemplate that which is beautiful. (8)

Having first demonstrated the fruits of *prāṇāyāma* and so forth, he describes the method of *prāṇāyāma* and the rest with the word "yathā" (just as): "Just as the impurities of mountain ores are burnt by the fire increased through smelting (*dhamana*), so too, by the retention of breath (*prāṇadhāraṇa*), the defects produced by the ten senses are burnt. (7) Since this is so, one should therefore burn the defects residing in the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) by means of *prāṇāyāmas*. Likewise, one should burn the blemish (*kilbiṣa*) located in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by means of the concentrations (*dhāraṇās*). Having thus brought about the destruction of the impurity born of the internal organ, one should contemplate the beautiful "Kumbhaka of all functions"—which is the suppression of the functions of mind and breath—as indicated by the word "hi" (indeed), which serves as the locus for the destruction of blemishes. (8)
The threefold breath control consists of the beautiful exhalation (recaka) and likewise the drawing in of the air;
these three breath controls are declared to be exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka).

He describes the threefold breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the words "the beautiful" (ruciram). Prāṇāyāmas are said to be of three kinds, distinguished by retention (kumbhaka), exhalation (recaka), and inhalation (pūraka). Here, the word "beautiful" (rucira) refers to retention (kumbhaka), because it is mentioned in conjunction with exhalation and inhalation. || 9 ||
One who has restrained the breath should recite three times the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras;
that is called Prāṇāyāma. (10)

He describes the nature of *prāṇāyāma*: "With the *vyāhṛtis*" and so forth. During the state of *kumbhaka*, one should recite the *gāyatrī* three times—that is, utter it mentally three times—along with the seven *vyāhṛtis* enclosed by the *praṇava* (e.g., *oṃ bhūḥ*) and together with the *śiras* mantra, "parorajase sāvadom. This is what is called *prāṇāyāma*. || 10 ||
Having raised the breath into space and made it empty and selfless,
one should employ it in the state of emptiness; such is the characteristic of *recaka*.

He states the definition of *recaka* (exhalation): "Having raised," etc. Having raised the air into the external space and having exhaled it very slowly, like a stream of oil, one should make the internal air selfless—that is, void—and fix it in the state of emptiness; this is the definition of *recaka*. || 11 ||
The characteristic of *pūraka* (inhalation) is as follows:
just as a person draws water through the stalk of a lotus with the mouth, so too should the air be grasped; this is the definition of *pūraka*.

He states the characteristic of *pūraka* (inhalation) with the words "by the mouth" (*vaktreṇa*). Just as a person might draw up water by means of the mouth or by the stalk of a lotus situated in the mouth, so too the air is to be grasped through the *iḍā*, the *piṅgalā*, or the *śītalinī*; this is the characteristic of *pūraka*. || 12 ||
The characteristic of *kumbhaka* is that one should neither exhale nor inhale, nor move the limbs; one should maintain such a state—this is the definition of *kumbhaka*. || 13 ||
"See forms as if blind; hear sound as if deaf;
see the body indeed as if it were wood—such is the characteristic of one who is perfectly tranquil. (14)

He states the definition of *kumbhaka* (retention) with the words "nor should he exhale" (*nochvased*). Having assumed a perfected posture (*siddhāsana*) and keeping the body motionless, the yogi, without performing the operations of exhalation (*recaka*) or inhalation (*pūraka*), should apply himself to the state of arresting the vital air (*vāyustambhana*). This is the definition of *kumbhaka*. (13) Regarding the definition of "tranquility" (*praśānta*), he says "like a blind man," meaning that during the time of *kumbhaka*, one should become devoid of engagement with forms, sounds, and so forth, like one who is blind or deaf. The mention of the blind and the deaf is intended to illustrate the impairment of the remaining sense organs as well. Just as a blind person or the like does not perceive form and so on, even though his senses are unimpaired, he should likewise view forms and so on as if he were blind, and view his own body as if it were a piece of wood. This is the characteristic of the tranquilized state. The meaning is that the yogi should become devoid of all sensory activity. (14)
Having meditated upon the mind, which has the nature of retention and is characterized by volition, the wise man should withdraw it into the self;
thus, having fixed the self [therein], it is proclaimed as *dhāraṇā* (retention). 15.

He states the definition of *dhāraṇā*: "The mind," etc. The wise yogi, having withdrawn the mind—which consists of volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*)—along with its entire range of modifications, and then having meditated upon that which is free from such constructs, fixes the Supreme Self in the same manner within the self, which is the non-conceptualizing mind transformed into the state of the inner witness (*pratyagbhāva*). That state of oneness between the inner witness and the Supreme is proclaimed as *dhāraṇā*. || 15 ||
The definition of reasoning (*tarka*):
Reasoning is said to be an inferential deliberation (*ūhana*) that is not in contradiction with scripture (*āgama*).
He states the definition of reasoning: "of scripture" (*āgamasya*). Only an inferential deliberation supported by revelation (*śruti*) is designated as reasoning.
That which one considers equal to the characteristic of meditative absorption (samādhi) once it has been attained—that is proclaimed as true meditative absorption. || 16 ||

He states the characteristic of samādhi: "Equal" (samam). Having realized that Supreme Self, thinking "I am Brahman; I alone am Brahman," one should regard the entire collection of the phenomenal world imagined by oneself as equal to the Self alone; this is proclaimed by the Śrutis as samādhi. || 16 ||
The means for accomplishing meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is as follows:
having performed mental protection upon a delightful seat of *darbha* grass on the ground, free from all defects, one should recite [the mantra] within the chariot-mandala (*rathamaṇḍala*). (17)
Having properly assumed a yogic posture— whether it be the lotus (padmaka), the swastika (svastika), or the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana)— he stands facing the north.
Having closed one nostril with the finger, one should draw in the air through the other and hold the fire; one should contemplate only the sound. (19)
"Oṃ" is the single-syllabled Brahman; one should not let this "Oṃ" slip away.
Through the divine mantra, one should perform [the rite] in many ways for the sake of liberation from impurity. (20)
Thereafter, the wise knower of mantras should meditate according to the previously described sequence;
beginning from the navel, he should contemplate the gross and the subtle, starting with the gross. (21)
Having abandoned the gaze directed sideways, upwards, or downwards, the one of great intelligence, remaining firm and unwavering, should always practice yoga. (22)
Being motionless for the duration of a palm tree's height (tāla), as well as the application of concentration (dhāraṇā) for that same measure;
yoga, however, is traditionally defined by the rule of twelve measures (mātras) in terms of time. || 23 ||

That syllable which is without sound, without consonants, and without vowels; which is produced neither by the palate, the throat, nor the lips, nor by the nose; which is not born from the letter *r*, and is devoid of both types of sibilants (*ūṣman*); that syllable does not perish in any way whatsoever. (24)

He states the means for the attainment of such *samādhi* with the words "on the ground" (*bhūmau*). This refers to a purified spot on the ground; the mention of a *darbha* seat is intended as an illustration for a seat made of *cīra*, deerskin, and so forth. On a soft seat made of *kuśa* grass, deerskin, or cloth—which is free from all defects—one should perform the purification of the ground and the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and having performed the mental protection (*rakṣā*) for the sake of purifying that [seat], one should touch that seat, and then recite the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the eight-syllabled solar mantra (*saura-aṣṭākṣara*) upon the chariot-mandala according to one's capacity. (17) Then, having sat down on that seat according to the rules, and having assumed one of the postures—such as the lotus (*padma*), the swastika (*svastika*), or the auspicious (*bhadra*)—one should sit properly facing north. (18) Covering one nostril with a hand having a finger placed upon it, one should draw in the breath and hold the fire within the triangle at the *mūlādhāra*; while holding it, one should contemplate only the sound of the syllable *Oṃ*. (19) What is that? It is "the single syllable *Om*" (*omityekākṣaram*). One should not allow the continuity of the contemplation of the *Oṃkāra* to be interrupted. For the sake of removing the impurities residing within one’s own internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), one should perform *japa* many times with the divine mantra. (20) Thus, the wise knower of the mantra should subsequently meditate according to the sequence previously described. The rule for the sequence of meditation is stated as "from the gross, etc. (*sthūlādīti*). Taking recourse to the gross and subtle aspects divided according to the Virāṭ, Sūtra, Bīja, and Turya forms—which serve as the locus for the superimposition and negation (*apavāda*) of the gross parts of the state of one's own ignorance—the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that one should also take recourse to the Bīja and Turya portions. One should begin the meditation on the Virāṭ and others in the heart and other centers located above one's navel. (21) Immediately after beginning the meditation on the Virāṭ and others, the great-minded yogi, abandoning the horizontal, upward, and downward gaze that is distinct from the nature of his own object of meditation—the word "and" (*ca*) indicating that he should become solely intent on that—remaining steady in the previously mentioned lotus posture, and being unshaken through the contemplation of his desired goal, with a mind one-pointed toward the goal, he should always maintain the contemplative realization: "I am the Virāṭ and the rest."

One should practice yoga thoroughly. (22) Regarding the rule for the measure of *kumbhaka*: "measure" (*mātrā*) refers to a duration of time that is steady according to the standards of the *Haṭha-śāstra*. Whether consisting of eight measures or seven measures—as it is well-known in the world—so should the application of breath-retention (*śvāsadhāraṇā*) be performed in *kumbhaka*. Likewise, in a full *kumbhaka*, the yoga is traditionally remembered as being regulated by twelve measures. However, the duration of those twelve measures here is traditionally held to consist of ninety-six measures, calculated by the natural time of inhalation and exhalation. The meaning is that for one who meditates on the essential nature during such a long-duration *kumbhaka*, there arises the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that Imperishable (*akṣara*). (23) What is that Imperishable? Is it composed of letters such as voiced sounds (*ghoṣa*)? To this he says: "It is voiceless" (*aghoṣam*). Voiced sounds are the vowels; that which is devoid of them is "voiceless. Consonants are the letters beginning with *ka*; that which is devoid of them is "without consonants. Likewise, it is "without vowels" (*asvara*), being free from vowels such as *a* and so forth. It is devoid of that which is manifested in the locations of the palate, throat, lips, and nose. It is "not produced by *ra*" (*arephajātam*), being free from the calculation of semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*). It is devoid of the sibilants and aspirates (*ubhayoṣman*) such as *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*. That which does not perish in any way—that alone is the Imperishable, which is perceived through the direct experience of the yogi. (24)
Since one perceives the path through the constant practice of yoga, by which the vital breath proceeds,
therefore one should practice that constantly for the sake of traversing the path. (25)

Since yoga is the cause for perceiving the path to one's own attainment, it is said that one should constantly practice that very yoga—expressed by the word "yena" (by which). That yogi perceives the path to his own attainment through that yoga; and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), together with the faculty of sight (*dṛk*) and the mind (*manas*) and the fire (*agni*), proceeds along that very same path. Since this is so, one should therefore practice that very yoga without negligence, solely for the purpose of traveling the path that leads to the attainment of that state. || 25 ||
The wise know there are seven gateways for attaining the state of dream:
the heart-gateway, the wind-gateway, and another, the head-gateway;
as well as the liberation-gateway, the cavity, the hollow, and the mandala. (26)

(21) To the question, "How many kinds of doors for attaining one's own Self are there?", it is said: "The door of the heart" (*hṛddvāram*). The door of the heart leads to the Virāṭ, because the Virāṭ has the cosmic egg as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) residing within the heart. The door of the vital air (*vāyudvāra*) leads to the Sūtra, because the vital air is of the nature of the Sūtra, according to the Śruti: "O Gautama, that [vital air] is indeed the thread. The door of the head (*mūrdhadvāra*) leads to the Bījeśvara, according to the Śruti: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality. When asked, "What else? it is said: the door of liberation (*mokṣadvāra*), which consists of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), leads to Brahman non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), because the realization of that [Brahman] is mediated by the door of the half-measure. The door of liberation is divided threefold. How so? The cavity (*bila*) consisting of the gross portion of the half-measure leads to the Turya-Virāṭ. The hollow space (*suṣira*) consisting of the subtle portion of the half-measure leads to the Turya-Sūtra. The sphere (*maṇḍala*) consisting of the seed-portion of the half-measure leads to the Turya-Bīja. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that there exists the well-known door of Kaivalya known as *Parā*, because that makes known Brahman alone, which is devoid of all counter-correlates (*niṣpratiyogika*). Thus, the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman know that there are seven doors for attaining one's own Self; this is the meaning. || 26 ||
The abandonment of fear and so forth:
"Fear, anger, as well as laziness, excessive sleep, excessive wakefulness, overeating, and fasting—the yogi should always avoid these. (27)

Anticipating the doubt—“If there is an abundance of obstacles such as fear and anger, how can success be achieved in this way?”—and stating that success will indeed come from the abandonment of fear, he says: “Fear... In this regard, it is said that through the vision of the fearless and so forth, the yoga of abandoning mental fluctuations such as fear occurs: “For one who is regulated in food and recreation, regulated in performing actions, and regulated in sleep and wakefulness, yoga arises which destroys suffering. (Yoga Sūtra 2.49)
Thus says the Smṛti. || 27 ||
The fruit of practice is correctly cultivated through this method, day after day, in gradual succession;
knowledge arises of itself within three months—of this there is no doubt. (28)
With four [steps] he beholds the gods; with five, his stride is extended.
By his own will, he attains absolute liberation (kaivalya) in the sixth month; of this there is no doubt.

He describes the intermediate and primary fruits for one who practices in this manner with the words "by this": By this method, for one who practices on the ground upon a delightful seat of *darbha* grass as previously mentioned, the knowledge of Brahman arises spontaneously—without instruction—within three months. (28) From four months of practice, one sees the gods such as Indra and others; from five months of practice, the expanded sequence beginning with Virāṭ is perceived. From six months of practice, one attains liberation (*kaivalya*) at will; there is no doubt in this matter—this is the meaning. (29)
The earthly [element] is five measures, while that of Varuṇa (water) is four measures;
the fiery one is three measures, and the airy one is two measures. || 30 ||

One should likewise contemplate space as having a single measure (ekamātra), but one should contemplate that which is beyond measure (amātra) through yoga. Regarding what is to be contemplated by yoga, he says: "the earthly" (pārthiva). The meaning is this: from the earthly element up to space, as each successive quality is withdrawn, there arises subtlety, inwardness, and pervasiveness. Thus, one should contemplate Brahman—which is established through the negation of the entire collection of elements and elemental derivatives characterized by such measures—as being "beyond measure" (amātra), the non-dual Self alone, free from all opposition.
The manner of reflection: having formed a connection through the mind, one should contemplate by means of the self within the self. (31)
The vital breath (prāṇa) measures thirty and a half finger-breadths; where it is established by the vital breaths, this is known as "the breath," the range of the external breath. || 32 ||

He describes the manner of that contemplation with the words "with the junction" (sadhim) || 31 || The vital breath (*prāṇa*), which moves through thirty and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), is established in the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) together with the vital functions such as speech and the rest. This very sphere, which is the domain of the external and cosmic (*ādhidaivika*) breath, is known as the internal (*ādhyātmika*) breath. When that [breath] dissolves along with the aggregate of its own sustaining organs into the space of the heart—which is the object of the inner light—that substratum of dissolution is Brahman, non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*). In that Brahman-Self, having effected a union (*saṃdhi*)—that is, oneness—with the inner self that illumines it by means of the mind transformed into the form of Brahman, one should contemplate that Brahman is one's own self alone, established through the negation of the qualified aspect residing in that oneness which depends upon the distinction between the inner and the supreme. || 32 ||
The measure of breaths in one day and night is thirteen thousand, one hundred and eighty, and ninety-nine lakhs. (33)

He states the measure of breaths completed in a day and night with the words "And eighty... etc. The number of exhalations and so forth, characterized by the count of one hundred thousand, one hundred and eighty-two, is calculated according to the measure of a day and night. However, in another Vedic scripture (Śruti), it is traditionally taught that for six days and nights, there are twenty-one thousand and six hundred [breaths]. The difference in the numbers appearing in these two modes is justified by the relative proportions of the body, such as childhood and so forth. For one who stands comfortably with firm limbs, the movement of the breath appears steady; for one who is the opposite, the opposite occurs. Thus, both [traditions] are consistent, for there is no contradiction—this is the meaning. || 33 ||
The locations of the vital breaths and so forth are as follows:
the *prāṇa* is situated in the heart; the *apāna*, moreover, is in the anus; the *samāna* is in the region of the navel; and the *udāna* rests in the throat. (34)
Vyāna, having pervaded all the limbs, remains there at all times.
Thus, he states the locations of prāṇa and the others which produce the breaths, beginning with the word "prāṇa. (34)
Now, regarding their distinctions of color:
the colors of the five [elements], beginning with Prāṇa, follow in sequence. (35)
The prāṇa-vāyu is proclaimed to be red in color, resembling a gem;
the apāna, however, is situated in its center, with a luster like the wrath of Indra.
But Samāna, situated between the two, has a luster white as cow's milk;
Udāna is pale-white, and Vyāna indeed has a radiance like that of a flame.
He states the distinctions of form and color for the vital breaths and so forth, beginning with "Now" (atha). || 35-7 ||
The supreme fruit of this is that when the vital wind (māruta) pierces through this mandala and ascends to the crown of the head,
wherever one may die, one is not born again.
"He is not born again"—this is the Upaniṣad. || 38 ||

Revealing the supreme fruit of the practice of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), he concludes with the words "of whom": for that seeker of liberation, the yogin, the vital breath (*māruta*)—such as *prāṇa* and the rest—by the power of practice [enters] this sphere (*maṇḍala*) of the heart and other centers which are to be presided over.

Having pierced through the crown of the head, that yogi who has reached such maturity—whether it be the *turya* or the *turyātīta* residing in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*)—attains [realization] as being nothing but his own Self (*svamātra*). In accordance with the scriptural teaching beginning with "Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste," wherever he may live or even die, he is not born again; the meaning is that simultaneously with the knowledge of Brahman, he becomes Brahman itself. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. The word "Upaniṣad" marks the conclusion of the *Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad*. || 38 ||
This clear commentary on the Nādopaniṣad has been written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra;
this work explaining the present Upaniṣad consists of one hundred and sixty verses.
Thus ends the commentary on the Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad, completing the twenty-first [treatise] in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
